comments.author: @NoMoreHandouts
comments.text: This is an EXTREMELY unfair portrayal of tiny homes. These are clearly either dinky, dumpy tiny homes, AI generated, overpriced, or inexperienced people trying to DIY OR hire workers without checking them out first. I have been researching tiny homes for about 10 years, and if they are constructed by a reputable tiny home builder or in a higher end tiny home community, they are often done right from the beginning. It cracks me up that you'd be comparing some girls' homes in a backyard compared to a spacious higher end model home in an established tiny home park where the homes are incredibly gorgeous and functional. These parks often get filled up because of demand, and if they are built right, are solid, and are maintained well, they will re-sell for good money. Also, the majority of tiny homes are NOT off grid. There are tens of thousands of people living in tiny homes that got out from under the grind a demanding job and a big mortgage, with much more time for their personal lives and their families. I have to question why you would feature the dregs of tiny homes with clueless owners in order to scare people away from them. For aging people on Social Security that live in a big house, they can sell their house, build the tiny home of their dreams, and pay space rent, which is a fraction of their benefit check and still have money left over. People just need to be informed about zoning, utilities, how to build, etc. before they get involved in it. No argument there. Most young people however cannot afford a traditional home. They don't stand a chance. Your argument is mute when you're talking about a tiny home versus living in your car or living with mom and dad. As far as tiny home companies going out of business, people just need to do their homework first... check the company's bankruptcy history, lawsuits, complaints, customer experiences, corporate history, and whether there are warning signs that deposits aren’t safe. There are plenty of long-standing good companies out there. Regarding them being too expensive, I'd rather pay $100,000 for a good tiny home than $500K for a shack of a "house."  Watching you shake your head with your sad sack face and poor content is something I plan to avoid in the future. As IF your disapproval is the end-all. Tiny homes are enhancing lives for people that need them and simply use their brain before purchasing!

comments.author: @paxzin8501
comments.text:
These people have no concept of 'tiny' living.  They are so used to large open spaces, and they need a 'crash course'.  They need to try living in a studio apartment, an RV, for a few months to see 'if or how' they'll be able to adapt'.  They usually have too much stuff, and tiny homes are about minimalistic living.  Yeah, it sounds great on paper, 'less bills, less utilities' perhaps even the ability to 'pickup and move' in some situations.  Try living in a hunting cabin, a fish camp, a van, or even in the back of a Uhaul for just a week.  If after the 3rd day, you are pulling your hair out, then 'tiny living' is probably not for you.  

I know that Home Depot, (and similar entities) often sell 'kits'.  Maybe a barn, garage, or storage area.  These are bare-bones and can cost around 33-45k as they are.  It would then be up to you, to pour the concrete, insulate the walls, run plumbing/electric, etc.  And these expenses should match the 33-45k, 'carpet, paint, lights, water heater, sink, counters, etc.'  Not as hard-math, but if you can only work on this project while maintaining your 40 hr/wk job, expect that it'll take about 1 week for each $1k of improvements.  That's right it could take 33-45 weeks to finish your TH.  Or, you can 'hire it out'.  Take lots of photos, get all of your certifications/inspections as soon as possible.  

Establish early with your building inspector, whether you are using a septic, well, off-grid power, or municipal services.  If possible, 'buy the land outright'   Don't finance the land and the home together.  If you ever hit a financial snag, you can hold off on the home, but you can't hold off on a 'land payment'.  In the meantime, you can rent a utility trailer, you often see these on construction sites, it where the 'foreman, supervisor, the paperwork, etc, reside in a 'office space'.  If you can live in that thing for 33-45 weeks, you are well on your way to moving into the 'big house' aka, your tinyhome.  

I get so sick of people bad-mouthing Tiny homes, because they themselves didn't think it all of the way through.  If you need a 20' Uhaul to move your stuff, you are not prepared for a tiny home.  If you've been paying $1500/month rent/mortgage, you are prepared for a tiny home.  If you have very few 'outdoor interests' you are not prepared.  You need to think of your TH, as a place to eat, sleep, and poop, and that's about it, anything beyond that is 'luxury'.  

I hope this helps.

comments.text:
I lived in a 320 sq. ft. apartment for a year. I lived there alone. It was horrible. At first it seemed cozy, but I live in a climate where it’s too hot to be outside half the year, so being crammed into the tiny space all summer long was miserable. There was no storage. The bedroom was only big enough for a double bed, with no room for even a small nightstand. I had to put my alarm clock on the floor in the doorway into the room. You walked through the bathroom to get from the kitchen/living room to the bedroom.

I’d recommend that anyone who wants to buy a tiny home rents an apartment or RV of the size you’re planning to buy. Live in that rental for a year, then decide if tiny-home living is right for you. I guarantee that most people will give up that dream very quickly.

I bought a 1,300 sq. ft. condo for $70,000 back around the turn of the millennium and I’ve never regretted it. It’s now worth five times what I paid for it, and it’s got plenty of space for two people.
